subject: currentaffairs
title: The Whistleblower's Family
question: Imagine someone discovers their own parent is doing something seriously wrong at work - something that could hurt other people if it continues, but reporting it would very likely cost the parent their job and hurt the whole family financially. Would you report it? What matters more here - loyalty to family, or doing the right thing for others?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: What to listen for is whether the child treats family loyalty and duty to strangers as genuinely competing values rather than assuming one obviously trumps the other. A strong answer might try to find a way to intervene without full public exposure, or admit real reluctance even while landing on reporting it. Push further by asking what changes if the parent's wrongdoing only might cause harm, versus definitely will.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Group Punishment
question: A teacher can't work out which pupil in the class broke an expensive piece of equipment, so decides the whole class will lose a privilege unless someone confesses. You know who did it, but they're not a close friend and they seem genuinely sorry. Do you tell the teacher?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child separates the unfairness of collective punishment from the separate question of whether they personally should tell on someone. The most thoughtful answers usually reject the teacher's method as unfair while still wrestling honestly with whether they'd speak up anyway. Ask what they would do differently if the whole class stood to lose something much more serious than a privilege.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Inherited Advantage
question: Two students apply for the same scholarship. One has had years of private tutoring their family could afford; the other has had none but shows more natural improvement over the year. If you were picking the winner, would you judge them on their raw score, or try to account for the advantages each one started with? Is that even possible to do fairly?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: A reflective answer recognises that raw scores and improvement each capture something real and neither is simply the fair measure. Watch for whether the child can propose any practical way of accounting for starting points without it becoming subjective or unmeasurable. Ask them what they would say to the tutored student if they lost the scholarship on these grounds.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Promise You Regret
question: You promise a friend you'll keep a secret before you know what it is. It turns out to be something that could put them in real danger if it stays secret. Do you keep your word, or break the promise to protect them? Does a promise still count if you didn't know what you were agreeing to?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: The strongest responses notice that a promise made in ignorance of its content is a different kind of promise, and are willing to say so rather than treating all promises as equally binding. Weaker answers just assert that a promise is a promise without engaging with the danger involved. Follow up by asking whether it matters if breaking the secret only protects the friend from mild embarrassment rather than real danger.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Punishing the Innocent to Deter the Guilty
question: Imagine a school announces that if any pupil is caught cheating again this year, the whole year group will lose a trip that everyone has been looking forward to, as a way of getting pupils to police each other. Is it ever right to threaten to punish innocent people in order to change the behaviour of a few?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can articulate why punishing people who did nothing wrong feels different from punishing the guilty, even when it might work as a deterrent. A genuinely reflective answer will concede the method might actually be effective while still objecting to it on principle. Ask what they would say to a pupil who did everything right and still lost the trip.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Lesser Evil
question: Imagine being in charge during a crisis where every option available will hurt someone - there's no option where nobody is harmed. How would you decide which harm is acceptable? Does it matter whether the harm is something you cause directly, or something you simply fail to prevent?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: This is a deliberately open, high-difficulty prompt, so listen for whether the child tries to build any kind of principle at all rather than freezing or refusing to engage. The distinction between actively causing harm and merely failing to prevent it is the crux, and a child who raises it unprompted is reasoning at a genuinely advanced level. Push with a concrete version of the scenario and ask them to actually decide, rather than staying comfortably abstract.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Second Chances
question: Someone who was once excluded from a previous school for bullying moves to your school and genuinely seems to have changed. A younger pupil is nervous around them because of what they've heard. Do people always deserve a second chance? Who decides when trust has been earned back?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can hold two things at once: that people can genuinely change, and that trust from someone who wasn't there to witness the change is not unreasonable. A weak answer picks one side flatly; a strong one asks what evidence of change would actually be convincing. Ask who they think should bear responsibility for managing that risk - the school, the new pupil, or the younger pupil who is nervous.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Talented Cheat
question: Imagine a brilliant athlete or musician is caught being dishonest in a way that has nothing to do with their talent - for example, cheating on an unrelated test. Should that change how we judge their achievements in the area where they're genuinely gifted? Or are the two things completely separate?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: A sophisticated answer separates the question of whether someone's talent is real from the question of whether they deserve praise or trust more broadly. Watch for a child who says something like the achievement is still real but it doesn't mean they're a good person - that's a meaningful distinction. Ask whether the answer changes if the dishonesty happened years before the achievement, rather than around the same time.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Loyalty to a Flawed Team
question: Your team is about to win an important match partly because the referee has made a mistake in your favour that nobody else has noticed. Do you say something? What if it were the other way round, and your team was about to lose because of the referee's mistake?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: The symmetry test in the second half of the question is the key part - listen for whether the child gives the same answer regardless of which team benefits from the referee's mistake. A child who admits they'd behave differently depending on who wins is being unusually honest, which is worth noting even though it's the less flattering answer. Ask what they think it says about fairness if most people would only speak up when it costs them nothing.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Doctor's Dilemma
question: Imagine a hospital has only one machine that can save a life, and two patients need it at the same time - one is a young child, one is an elderly scientist close to finishing research that could help thousands of future patients. How should a decision like that be made? Is it ever right to weigh whose life matters more?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child resists the urge to find an easy way out of the dilemma, such as getting a second machine, and instead actually grapples with the comparison being asked. The strongest answers question whether it's ever legitimate to weigh lives by their expected future contribution, rather than just picking an answer. Ask whether their reasoning would change if the scientist's research success were only a possibility rather than a near-certainty.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Deserved Consequences
question: Someone works incredibly hard their whole life but has a small amount of bad luck and ends up failing; someone else works far less hard but succeeds because of good luck. Do you think people generally get what they deserve in life? Does effort matter more than outcome when we judge someone's worth?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: A strong answer separates what people deserve morally for their effort from what actually happens to them, rather than assuming the two must line up. Listen for whether the child brings in the idea of luck unprompted, since younger children often default to a pure effort-equals-reward view. Ask whether we should judge people's worth by effort even when the world doesn't reward it that way.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Unfair Advantage You Didn't Ask For
question: Imagine you found out that you'd been given a place at a school partly because of a small clerical error that worked in your favour, and nobody else knows. Would you say something, even though undoing it would be very difficult? Does it matter if speaking up wouldn't undo any harm to anyone else?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child treats not having caused the error as a full excuse for staying silent, or recognises that knowingly benefiting from an unfair error is its own separate choice. The most honest answers admit this would be a genuinely difficult thing to give up, rather than claiming it would be easy. Ask whether their answer changes if speaking up would mean someone else, who missed out because of the error, gets the place instead.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The AI Companion
question: Some apps now offer AI companions designed to be endlessly supportive, patient and available in a way real friends often aren't. If a lonely person found genuine comfort talking to one every day, would that be a good thing, a bad thing, or does it depend? What might it cost them, even if it makes them feel better in the moment?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can name a specific cost of AI companionship beyond a vague sense that it's not real, such as it never challenging the person or never having its own needs. The strongest answers avoid simply dismissing the comfort as fake, since it can genuinely help someone in the moment, while still identifying what's missing compared to a human relationship. Ask what they'd say to someone who told them the AI understood them better than any person ever had.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Grading by Algorithm
question: Imagine exam grades were decided partly by an algorithm that predicts how well a student would have done, based on things like their school's past results and their coursework history, rather than purely by the exam itself. Would that be fairer or less fair than relying only on the exam? What could go wrong either way?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child identifies the specific risk that an algorithm using school-level data could unfairly cap or inflate an individual student's outcome based on group patterns that don't apply to them personally. A strong answer weighs this against the fact that exams themselves are also imperfect and can be affected by one bad day. Ask them what safeguard, if any, would make an algorithm like this acceptable to them.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Right to Be Forgotten
question: Should someone be able to demand that true information about something embarrassing or damaging they did years ago be removed from the internet, even though it actually happened? Where's the line between someone's right to move on and the public's right to know the truth?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can propose any kind of line, such as time passed, age at the time, or the seriousness of what happened, rather than treating this as all-or-nothing. The strongest answers notice that this isn't really a technology question at all, but an old question about redemption and record-keeping wearing new clothes. Ask whether their answer changes if the information in question is about someone applying for a position of real public trust.

subject: currentaffairs
title: AI Making the Final Call
question: Imagine a hospital uses an AI system that's proven to be more accurate than human doctors at diagnosing a serious illness, but sometimes gets individual cases wrong in ways doctors find hard to explain. Should the final decision on a patient's treatment ever be left entirely to the AI, even though on average it saves more lives than a human would? What do we lose if a human is no longer making the actual call?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child engages with the actual trade-off - that following the more accurate AI on average will save more lives overall, even though it will get some individual cases wrong that a human might have caught. A genuinely strong answer identifies that the objection isn't really about accuracy at all, but about accountability and the ability to explain a decision to the person affected by it. Ask what they would want to happen if the AI's recommendation and their own doctor's judgement directly disagreed.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Deepfake of You
question: Imagine incredibly realistic video and audio could be generated of anyone, including you, saying or doing things you never actually said or did, and it's now genuinely hard to prove what's fake. What responsibility, if any, do individual people have to help solve this problem, versus governments or the companies that build the technology?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child avoids the easy move of putting all responsibility on the technology companies and actually considers what an ordinary individual could realistically do, such as how they verify what they see and share. The strongest answers acknowledge that this is a genuinely hard collective action problem rather than pretending there's a simple fix. Ask what they would actually do if a convincing fake video of them started circulating at school.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Automating Away the Ladder
question: Many of the entry-level jobs that people traditionally used to learn a trade or profession - junior roles where you make small mistakes and learn from them - are increasingly being done by AI. If that trend continues, how do people gain the experience needed for the more senior jobs that still need humans? Is this a problem we should try to slow down, or just adapt to?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child grasps that this isn't simply AI taking jobs, but a subtler problem about how people gain the specific experience senior roles require in the first place. A strong answer considers who has responsibility for fixing this - employers, schools, individuals - rather than only describing the problem. Ask whether they think this is a temporary transition problem or a permanent change to how people learn to work.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Should AI Companies Slow Down?
question: Some people who build AI systems argue that the technology should be developed as fast as possible so that the benefits - curing diseases, solving big problems - arrive sooner. Others say it should be slowed down deliberately so society has time to catch up with safety and regulation. If you had to pick a side, which risk worries you more: moving too fast, or moving too slowly?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can name a genuine cost to the option they don't pick, rather than treating their chosen side as risk-free. The most sophisticated answers notice that speeding up and slowing down aren't just about a dial, but about who gets to decide the pace and how that decision is enforced globally. Ask what they would do if only one country agreed to slow down while others carried on at full speed.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Algorithm That Knows You Too Well
question: Apps that recommend videos, music or products often get scarily good at predicting exactly what you'll enjoy next. Is that a good thing because it saves you time and effort, or a bad thing because it narrows what you're exposed to without you really choosing that? Have you noticed this happening to you?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child brings genuine personal experience into the answer, since this question is partly testing self-awareness about their own digital habits. A strong answer distinguishes between the recommendation being accurate and it being good for them, which are not the same thing. Ask them to describe a specific moment they noticed an algorithm influencing what they thought or wanted.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Who's Responsible When AI Gets It Wrong?
question: If a self-driving car makes a decision that causes an accident, who should be held responsible - the company that built it, the engineer who wrote the specific piece of code, the owner of the car, or nobody in particular because it was a genuine accident? Does it matter that no single person actually decided what the car would do in that exact moment?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child resists picking a single tidy answer and instead recognises that responsibility might need to be shared or split in a new way for this kind of technology. A weaker answer just says the company without explaining why that's fairer than blaming the individual engineer or owner. Ask whether their answer would change if the accident happened because the owner ignored a safety update they were told to install.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Digital Twins of the Dead
question: Imagine AI tools exist that can recreate a realistic chatbot version of someone who has died, trained on their messages and voice recordings, so grieving family members can keep talking to them. Would you consider that a comfort worth having, or something that stops people moving on and processing loss properly?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can hold both the genuine comfort and the genuine risk in mind at once, rather than dismissing the idea outright or endorsing it without reservation. The most thoughtful answers distinguish between using it briefly during acute grief versus relying on it indefinitely as a substitute for accepting the loss. Ask what they think the difference is between this and simply looking at old photos or videos of someone who has died.

subject: currentaffairs
title: AI and the Truth
question: If an AI system can generate incredibly convincing arguments for almost any position, including ones that are false or misleading, how do you think people will decide what to believe in future? Is the solution better technology to detect fakes, better education, or something else entirely?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child recognises that this is fundamentally a human problem of trust and judgement that technology alone cannot fully solve, even if it can help. The strongest answers propose something concrete, such as changes to what's taught in schools or how information is labelled, rather than a vague call for better regulation. Ask how they personally decide whether to trust something convincing that they've read or watched.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Fair Use of a Limited Resource
question: Training and running powerful AI systems uses a huge amount of energy and water for cooling data centres, at a time when we're also trying to cut emissions and conserve resources. Should there be limits on how much AI development is allowed to consume, even if it slows down useful progress? Or is that resource cost worth paying?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child weighs the environmental cost against genuinely useful outcomes of AI, rather than treating all AI use as equally worthwhile or equally wasteful. A strong answer might distinguish between AI used for something like medical research and AI used for something trivial. Ask who they think should decide which uses of AI are worth the environmental cost.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Free Speech You Disagree With
question: Should someone be allowed to publicly say things that are offensive or that you strongly disagree with, as long as they're not directly inciting violence? Where do you personally draw the line between protecting free speech and protecting people from harm?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can draw an actual line rather than a vague gesture towards one, since saying it depends on how extreme it is isn't really a line at all. The strongest answers give a specific test, such as direct incitement to violence versus causing offence, and can explain why that particular boundary makes sense. Ask them to apply their own rule to a specific example and see if it still holds up.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Quota Question
question: Imagine a university reserves a certain number of places each year specifically for students from backgrounds that are usually underrepresented, even if it means a handful of students with slightly higher grades from more advantaged backgrounds don't get in. Is that fair? Does fairness mean treating everyone identically, or accounting for different starting points?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child engages with both definitions of fairness in play here - identical treatment versus accounting for different starting points - rather than assuming only one is the real meaning of fairness. A genuinely strong answer acknowledges that the students who narrowly miss out have a real grievance, even if they ultimately support the policy. Ask what they think should happen once genuine equality of opportunity has actually been achieved.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Privacy vs Safety in Schools
question: Should schools be allowed to monitor students' private messages and browsing on school-issued devices in order to catch bullying or safeguarding problems early, even though it means reading things students assumed were private? What if it occasionally catches something completely unrelated and personal?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child considers the effect of constant monitoring on students who aren't doing anything wrong, not just the benefit for the cases where something is caught. A strong answer might propose some kind of limit on what's monitored or who can see it, rather than an all-or-nothing position. Ask whether their answer changes if the monitoring is announced openly in advance versus done without students knowing.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Housing the Many vs the Few
question: A city needs to build many more homes to solve a housing shortage, but the only available land is a small, much-loved green space that a handful of local residents have used for decades. Should the wider need of the many outweigh the loss to the few who actually use that space regularly?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child treats the residents' loss as trivial simply because they're a minority, or actually grapples with why a long-used local space might matter in ways that are hard to put a number on. The strongest answers consider whether compensation or an alternative site changes the fairness of the trade-off. Ask them what would change their mind if the green space were the only one nearby for people without gardens.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Burden of Proof
question: In most justice systems, someone is presumed innocent until proven guilty, which sometimes means people who are actually guilty go free because there isn't enough evidence. Is that trade-off the right one, or should the system sometimes lean the other way to make sure fewer guilty people escape, even if it risks convicting more innocent people?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child understands that this is a trade-off with no error-free option, since any system will occasionally get an innocent person convicted or a guilty person acquitted. A strong answer explains which mistake they think is worse and why, rather than just asserting the system should be fixed. Ask them what would happen to public trust in the justice system if it were seen to convict people on weaker evidence.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Equal Rules, Unequal Starting Points
question: Is it fairer to treat everyone exactly the same, following identical rules regardless of circumstances, or to make exceptions for people whose circumstances are genuinely different? Can you think of a rule at your school that you think should sometimes have exceptions?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can give a specific, real example rather than only speaking in the abstract, since the question is partly testing whether they can apply the principle to their own life. A strong answer recognises the downside of exceptions too - that they can be applied unevenly or unfairly by whoever's in charge of granting them. Ask who they'd trust to decide when an exception is genuinely deserved.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Who Gets to Decide What's Offensive?
question: Standards about what language or jokes are acceptable change a lot between generations and cultures. If something was considered completely normal to say twenty years ago and is now considered unacceptable, should we judge people from the past by today's standards, or by the standards of their own time?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child avoids the two easy extremes - judging the past entirely by today's standards, or excusing anything because it was a different time. The strongest answers try to separate the person's intent and the information available to them at the time from the actual impact of what they said or did. Ask whether people alive today making similar mistakes deserve the same leniency future generations might extend to us.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Tax on Success
question: Should people who earn a lot more money pay a much higher percentage of it in tax to fund things like the NHS and schools for everyone, or does that unfairly punish people for working hard and taking risks? Is there a point where higher taxes stop being fair and start being a disincentive?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can articulate the incentive argument on both sides - that high earners might work less or leave if taxed heavily, but also that public services depend on that revenue. A strong answer tries to locate roughly where the fair but not punishing line sits, rather than only picking a side in the abstract. Ask what they think should happen to someone who earns their money through luck, like winning it, versus through decades of work.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Protest and Disruption
question: Some protest movements deliberately disrupt everyday life, such as blocking roads or public transport, to draw attention to a cause they believe is urgent and important. Is that a legitimate way to campaign for change, even though it inconveniences or harms people who have nothing to do with the issue? Does the importance of the cause change your answer?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child's answer depends on whether they personally agree with the cause being protested, and whether they notice that dependency themselves. The strongest answers try to build a principle that would apply consistently, regardless of which cause is doing the disrupting. Ask whether they'd still defend the tactic if it were being used for a cause they found genuinely wrong.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Merit or Need?
question: If a school has one remaining bursary place for the next year, should it go to the student with the strongest grades, or the student who needs the financial help the most, even if their grades are a bit weaker? Can a selection process ever really separate the two?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child notices that grades themselves are partly a product of need and circumstance, which complicates treating merit and need as fully separate categories. A strong answer might propose a way of weighing both rather than choosing one exclusively. Ask them how they'd explain the decision to the student who wasn't chosen, whichever way they decide.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Right to Change Your Mind
question: Should someone be allowed to publicly hold and argue for a view, and then later change their mind completely without being mocked or accused of being untrustworthy for it? Or does changing your position on something important always cost you some credibility?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child distinguishes between changing your mind because of new evidence or genuine reflection, versus changing it purely for convenience or to avoid criticism. A strong answer recognises that the two look similar from the outside, which is part of what makes trust hard to maintain. Ask them whether they'd view a politician who changed a major policy position differently from a friend who changed a personal opinion.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Majority Rule vs Minority Rights
question: In a democracy, decisions are usually made by majority vote. But what happens when the majority votes for something that seriously disadvantages a small minority group who never had enough votes to stop it? Is majority rule always the fairest way to make decisions, or does it need limits?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can articulate what kind of limit on majority rule they think is justified, such as basic rights that can't be voted away, rather than just saying it depends. The strongest answers notice the tension between respecting democratic decisions and protecting people who will always be outvoted on issues that affect them most. Ask who should decide where those limits sit, if not the majority itself.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Cost of Cleaning Up
question: Imagine switching a whole country's energy system away from fossil fuels would mean thousands of people currently working in those industries lose their jobs, at least for a while, before new green jobs replace them. Is it fair to ask those specific workers and their families to bear that cost for a benefit that helps everyone? Who should pay to support them through the transition?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child recognises that a policy can be right for society overall while still being genuinely unfair to specific individuals within it, and that these aren't contradictory. A strong answer proposes some concrete way of sharing that cost more broadly, such as retraining support or compensation, rather than just accepting the harm as necessary collateral. Ask what they'd say to a worker who did everything right in their career and still lost their livelihood to the transition.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Rich Country, Poor Country
question: Wealthy countries built much of their prosperity using fossil fuels over the last two hundred years, and are largely responsible for the emissions causing climate change today. Poorer countries are now being asked to develop using cleaner, more expensive energy instead of the cheap fossil fuels that helped richer countries grow. Is that fair?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child brings historical responsibility into the answer unprompted, since this question is really testing whether they think fairness has to account for how we got here, not just where we are now. A strong answer might suggest wealthier countries should help fund cleaner development elsewhere, rather than simply restricting poorer countries' choices. Ask whether their answer changes if the poorer country could develop faster and more cheaply by using fossil fuels than any clean alternative available to it.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Population Question
question: Some people argue that the number of people on the planet is a major driver of environmental pressure, and that having fewer children is one of the most effective things an individual can do for the planet. Is it reasonable to bring personal choices like family size into environmental debates, or does that cross into places it shouldn't go?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: This is a deliberately sensitive question, so listen for whether the child can discuss it thoughtfully without either dismissing it entirely or drifting into something uncomfortable about who should or shouldn't have children. The strongest answers separate the environmental arithmetic from any judgement about individual family choices being anyone else's business. Ask them where they think the line is between raising awareness of an issue and pressuring people's personal decisions.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Nuclear Power
question: Nuclear power produces almost no carbon emissions and can generate huge amounts of reliable energy, but it creates radioactive waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years and carries a small risk of catastrophic accidents. Should countries build more nuclear power stations to fight climate change, accepting that risk? How do you weigh a small chance of a huge disaster against a near-certain climate benefit?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can reason about probability and scale together, rather than reacting purely to the word radioactive or purely to the word carbon-free. A strong answer might compare this risk to other risks society already accepts, such as those from fossil fuel pollution, to see if the comparison holds up. Ask what would change their mind about the acceptable level of risk.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Saving a Species vs Local Livelihoods
question: Imagine protecting an endangered species requires banning an activity, like fishing or farming, that a local community has relied on for generations to survive. Should the species be protected even if it means real hardship for the people living there? Does it matter that the community didn't cause the species to become endangered in the first place?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child considers alternatives beyond a strict ban, such as compensation or alternative livelihoods for the community, rather than treating it as a straight either-or choice. The strongest answers notice the fairness problem embedded in the question - that the people paying the cost usually aren't the ones who caused the species to become endangered. Ask whether their answer changes if the community's activity is the last remaining threat to the species' survival, versus one of several.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Flying and Fairness
question: Air travel produces a large amount of emissions per person, but for many people flying is the only realistic way to visit family abroad, see the world, or access opportunities. Should there be limits on how much any individual is allowed to fly, or restrictions that make flying much more expensive? Would that unfairly affect people who can't afford it already, or people who genuinely need to fly?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child distinguishes between flying for necessity, such as seeing family who live abroad, and flying for pure leisure, since a flat restriction affects these very differently. A strong answer might propose a way of pricing or limiting flights that accounts for that difference rather than treating all flights identically. Ask whether their answer changes for someone who only ever flies once every few years to see family, versus someone who flies frequently for holidays.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Geoengineering as a Backup Plan
question: Some scientists are researching technology that could deliberately intervene in the Earth's climate system, for example reflecting some sunlight away to cool the planet, as a backup if emissions cuts aren't happening fast enough. Should we develop this kind of technology as insurance, even though we don't fully understand what side effects it might cause? Or does having a backup plan reduce the pressure to fix the root cause?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child engages with the moral hazard argument - that having a backup plan might reduce the political pressure to cut emissions in the first place - rather than only discussing the direct technical risk. The strongest answers recognise that both researching it and refusing to research it at all carry real risks, and try to weigh them against each other rather than picking the more comfortable-sounding option. Ask what they'd want to happen if early tests suggested the technology worked but had unpredictable regional side effects.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Growth vs the Planet
question: Economic growth has lifted huge numbers of people out of poverty, but it's also closely linked to rising emissions and resource use. Is it possible to keep growing economies while genuinely protecting the environment, or is there a point where we have to choose one over the other? If you had to choose, which would you prioritise?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child questions the premise itself - whether growth and environmental protection are actually always in conflict, or whether that depends on the kind of growth - rather than simply accepting the trade-off as given. A strong answer that does pick a side explains what it would mean in practice for people currently living in poverty. Ask them whether their answer would be different if they themselves were living in a country still trying to lift people out of poverty.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Who Should Pay for Climate Disasters?
question: When extreme weather linked to climate change devastates a poorer country that contributed very little to causing the problem, should wealthier, high-emitting countries be required to pay for the damage and recovery? Or is that an impossible thing to fairly calculate and enforce?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child separates the moral question of who's responsible from the practical question of how such a system could actually be calculated and enforced fairly. A strong answer acknowledges both difficulties rather than dismissing the practical objection as an excuse to avoid the moral one. Ask how they would decide how far back in history responsibility for emissions should count.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Small Actions, Big Systems
question: Individual actions like recycling or eating less meat make only a tiny difference compared to changes made by large industries and governments. Does that mean individual choices don't really matter for climate change, or is there still a reason to make them?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can articulate a reason for individual action that doesn't depend on it making a measurable difference on its own, such as its effect on social norms or personal integrity. A weaker answer either overstates how much individual choices matter or concludes they're pointless and therefore not worth doing. Ask them whether they'd still make the same personal choices if they knew for certain nobody else would ever find out.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Protecting Nature vs Feeding People
question: Imagine a country with a fast-growing population needs to clear forest land to grow more food, but that forest absorbs large amounts of carbon and is home to species found nowhere else. Should feeding people today take priority over protecting an ecosystem for the future? Is there a way to think about this that doesn't just pick one side?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child resists collapsing this into a simple choice and instead considers whether there's a version of food production that doesn't require clearing that specific forest, even if it's more expensive or difficult. The strongest answers notice that framing this as people versus nature can obscure who specifically benefits from each option and who pays the cost. Ask whether their answer changes if the food grown would mostly be exported rather than feeding the local population.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Deadline Problem
question: Scientists often give specific deadlines, such as a certain number of years, before some climate damage becomes irreversible. But predictions like that are always somewhat uncertain, and past deadlines have sometimes been missed without total catastrophe. How should uncertain but serious warnings like this affect what we do today? Should we act as if the worst-case prediction is definitely true?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can act sensibly under genuine uncertainty rather than either dismissing warnings because they're not perfectly precise or treating every prediction as guaranteed fact. A strong answer might reference the idea of managing risk even without certainty, similar to why people wear seatbelts without knowing they'll crash. Ask what they think we should do differently if scientists later revise a deadline to be much less urgent than first thought.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The News You Trust
question: How do you decide whether a news source is trustworthy? Is it possible to be well-informed about the world without accidentally absorbing a particular bias, given that almost every source has one?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child names a specific, practical habit, such as comparing multiple sources or checking who funds a publication, rather than a vague claim like just knowing what's true. The strongest answers accept that some bias is probably unavoidable and describe how they try to account for that, rather than claiming to have solved it. Ask them to name a source they trust and explain honestly what bias it might have.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Sanctions That Hurt Ordinary People
question: When one country imposes economic sanctions on another to pressure its government over its actions, it's often ordinary citizens, not the leaders responsible, who suffer the most from the resulting shortages and economic hardship. Are sanctions like this still justified as a tool of foreign policy, even knowing who actually bears the cost?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child grapples honestly with the fact that a tool can be somewhat effective and still cause real harm to people who had no power over the decisions being punished. A strong answer might explore whether there are more targeted alternatives, rather than treating it as sanctions versus doing nothing at all. Ask what they think should happen if the sanctions clearly aren't changing the government's behaviour but are still hurting ordinary citizens.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Should Countries Take In More Refugees?
question: When conflict or disaster forces large numbers of people to flee their homes, wealthier countries face pressure to take in refugees, but doing so at scale can strain housing, public services and local communities that are already stretched. How should a country decide how many people it can reasonably take in, and who decides what 'reasonable' means?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child treats this as a real capacity question with genuine limits, rather than either an unlimited moral obligation or a purely closed door. The strongest answers try to describe what reasonable might actually depend on, such as available housing, services, or economic conditions, rather than leaving the word undefined. Ask who they think should have the final say when local communities and national government disagree about how many people can be accommodated.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Boycotts and Consequences
question: If a company or country does something you find morally wrong, is boycotting them, refusing to buy their products or engage with them, an effective and fair way to respond, or does it mostly end up hurting ordinary employees and workers who had no say in the decision?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child weighs the intended pressure on decision-makers against the likely, more diffuse harm to ordinary workers, rather than assuming a boycott only affects the people responsible. A strong answer might distinguish between boycotts aimed at specific decision-makers versus broad boycotts of an entire company or country. Ask whether they'd still support a boycott if they learned it was mostly costing jobs for people who agreed with the boycotters' cause.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Cost of Neutrality
question: When a serious conflict or injustice is happening somewhere in the world, is it acceptable for a country, or a person, to stay neutral and not take a side? Or is choosing not to get involved itself a kind of choice, with its own consequences?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child considers that declining to take a side can itself have real consequences, rather than treating neutrality as automatically the safe or blameless option. A strong answer might distinguish between situations where neutrality helps de-escalate conflict and situations where it effectively favours whoever holds more power. Ask them to apply their view to a specific situation where staying out of it clearly benefited one side over the other.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Trade-off Between Security and Freedom
question: After a serious security threat, governments sometimes introduce new surveillance powers or restrictions on freedoms that they say are necessary to keep people safe. How much freedom do you think it's reasonable to give up for extra safety, and who should decide when the government has gone too far?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can name a specific freedom they'd be willing to give up and one they wouldn't, rather than answering only in the abstract. The strongest answers address who should have the power to decide when a threat justifies new restrictions, and how those restrictions get rolled back once the threat passes. Ask whether temporary emergency powers, once granted, tend to actually go away again.

subject: currentaffairs
title: When Should a Country Intervene Abroad?
question: If a government is seriously mistreating its own citizens, should other countries be allowed to intervene, even militarily, to try to stop it, even though that means interfering in another country's internal affairs without being asked? What's the difference between protecting people and imposing your own values on someone else's country?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child can articulate a principle distinguishing legitimate humanitarian intervention from an excuse to interfere for other reasons, rather than deciding case by case with no consistent rule. A strong answer grapples honestly with the fact that intervention can also make a bad situation worse. Ask what should happen if the country being asked to help has its own history of interfering in others' affairs for less noble reasons.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Fast Fashion and Global Supply Chains
question: Cheap clothing keeps prices low for shoppers, including families who can't afford more expensive alternatives, but it's often produced in factories with poor pay and working conditions overseas. Is it reasonable to expect individual shoppers to pay more to fix this, or is that really a problem only governments and companies can solve?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child recognises the tension between affordability for lower-income shoppers at home and fair conditions for lower-income workers abroad, rather than treating only one group's hardship as real. A strong answer might propose where responsibility should sit, among consumers, companies, or governments, and explain why. Ask them whether they personally think about this when they buy something cheap, and if not, why not.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Misinformation and Who Gets to Correct It
question: Should social media companies be responsible for removing false information from their platforms, even political claims, or does that give a small number of private companies too much power over what people are allowed to see and believe?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child weighs the genuine harm misinformation causes against the risk of concentrating the power to decide truth in a small number of companies. A strong answer might propose some kind of check on that power, such as transparency or appeal processes, rather than a simple yes or no. Ask who they'd trust to make that call if not the platforms themselves.

subject: currentaffairs
title: The Automation of Ordinary Jobs
question: As AI and automation take over more everyday jobs, from driving to customer service, some people will need to retrain into completely different careers, sometimes more than once in their working life. Is that a reasonable expectation to place on people, or should society find a different way to support people whose jobs disappear through no fault of their own?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child considers the practical difficulty of retraining repeatedly through a working life, the time, cost, and uncertainty involved, rather than treating retraining as a simple solution. A strong answer might propose what kind of support should exist, such as funded retraining or a different economic safety net entirely. Ask them what they'd say to someone in their fifties whose entire career has just been automated away.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Should Historical Wrongs Be Compensated Today?
question: Some people argue that countries or institutions that benefited from historical injustices, such as colonialism, owe some form of compensation to the descendants of those harmed, even generations later. Others argue that people today shouldn't be held responsible for wrongs committed by people long dead. Where do you stand, and why?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child separates responsibility for causing harm from the separate question of who benefits today from wrongs committed generations ago. The strongest answers notice that people today didn't do it and some people today still benefit from it can both be true at once, and try to reason from there rather than picking whichever fact is more convenient. Ask what kind of compensation, if any, they think could actually address a wrong from that long ago.

subject: currentaffairs
title: Voting for Someone You Don't Fully Trust
question: In an election, is it better to vote for the candidate whose policies you agree with most, even if you have doubts about their honesty or character, or to prioritise trustworthiness over specific policies? Can you actually separate the two?
answer: Discussion question — there is no single correct answer. Assess the reasoning, honesty and perspective-taking, not a 'right' response.
modelReasoningPath: Listen for whether the child recognises that policy promises depend on trust to be delivered at all, which complicates cleanly separating the two factors. A strong answer might describe a personal threshold, a level of dishonesty that would override any policy agreement, rather than treating trust as infinitely tradeable against policy. Ask them what they'd do if the more trustworthy candidate had policies they found seriously harmful.
